entries.title: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
entries.summary: The blockbuster game makes no secret of its contempt for law enforcement. Real police departments using it to recruit new members and scold the public apparently didn’t get the memo.
entries.content:
Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.

An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”

Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

Among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”

The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip showed a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.

A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.

Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.

Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.

More baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.

What do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

entries.title: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
entries.summary: Amid allegations of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, sources tell WIRED the Nvidia board’s main issue was the former CEO’s “lack of candor.”
entries.content:
Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said.

In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact WIRED reporters securely on Signal at ChaoticGoode.12 & Peard33.24

Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”

Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.”

The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” says one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”

At the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.

“The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”

entries.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
entries.summary: A supermajority of eligible workers at the nonprofit digital library voted in favor of joining the Communications Workers of America.
entries.content:
Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.

Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”

The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI.

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.)

Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”

Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.

entries.title: Don’t Bring Jensen Back
entries.summary: A mob of tech bros is clamoring for Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. It’s a bad idea.
entries.content:
Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.

Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.

Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.

It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?

The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.

At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.

Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.

The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?)

There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.

On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”

Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.

Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

entries.title: The Best Pura Deals for Cyber Week (2026)
entries.summary: Pura fragrances are 20 percent off, and diffusers are 30 percent off through December 6. Here’s what I’d buy after having tested three generations of Pura devices.
entries.content:
Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser. Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work by blowing air through oil) for years due to its ease of use and sprawling library of high-end scents.

In fact, no brand even comes close to Pura's sheer breadth of available fragrances—with more than 150 options from big names like Anthropologie, Nest, LAFCO, Brooklyn Candle Company, Studio McGee, and more. Pura even has special seasonal collabs, like this month’s Nutcracker-inspired scents from the New York City Ballet. These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).

But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo. (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.)

Cartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.

Worth the Buy

Pura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (though I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no issues in six months of testing.

If you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the new Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.

I also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.

There’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale (MSRP averages $21 apiece, and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.

Also on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar, which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.

Another Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces, which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). However, it did do a great job of scenting a high-ceilinged room on the first floor of my house.

entries.title: The Birdfy Gifts I’d Buy for Backyard Birders
entries.summary: After more than two years of testing smart bird feeders, these are the picks I’d give others, including a simple camera feeder and a nest box that let me watch chickadees raise their young.
entries.content:
I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most. These feeders are well-made, reliable, and reasonably priced. The brand's app is also excellent; it's easy to navigate and use without shelling out for an additional subscription. Better still, Birdfy just rolled out free lifetime AI ID (which is quite decent) with any bird feeder, including the lowest-priced models. If you don't want to gift a traditional feeder, you might consider Birdfy's smart birdbath and nesting box, each of which comes equipped with the same high-quality camera(s).

Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.

Featured Gifts

The One That Started It All

WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022. Back then we loved the concept, but felt its AI ID didn't quite cut it. Birdfy has come a long way since then on the AI front. The feeder body is largely the same, but the app and AI ID (now free) are both much improved, offering a seamless and user-friendly experience that makes it easy to sort through which birds visited that day. This once-pricey feeder is now at the lowest price I have ever seen for the version without the solar panel. The 5200-mAh rechargeable battery lasts a few weeks, but I think it's convenient to not have to bring it in to charge, if you want to spring for the extra $20 for that solar panel.

A Solid Budget Option

Birdfy's “beginner” model, this unit is basically a gravity pet feeder with a camera on the side. All you need to do is snap three pieces together, charge the camera, and pair it to the Birdfy app. If you know anyone who loves birds but is intimidated by the thought of having to set up and calibrate a smart bird feeder, this could be the perfect gift for them. However, note that my test unit keeps losing its lid on windy days, and there's no roof to keep the seed from getting wet on rainy days, so it's probably best for summer use. I also just discovered that Walmart carries an exclusive periwinkle color that looks lovely.

New and Improved

Birdfy's Metal 2 4K is the brand's flagship release for this year, with Ultra 4K resolution and dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi connection. The metal body claims to resist squirrels, and the muted green color is a welcome change from Birdfy's usual bright plastics. As was the case with the brand's previous flagship, the Feeder 2 Pro, I had some significant connection issues with the Metal 2 4K. This kept it from being a top pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, but the model is still worth a mention here due to its combination of features and build quality, as well as Birdfy's excellent customer service if something does go wrong.

Best Looking

Smart bird feeders aren't always the most aesthetically pleasing thing you could put in your yard, but Birdfy's 2K bamboo model was the first smart feeder I've ever had that actually garnered compliments. The natural wood and waterfall-style black roof complement any landscaping or exterior decor, and the camera and overall setup ran flawlessly for me during my months of testing. Just make sure you apply varnish or urethane regularly to the bamboo, as the finish on mine peeled after only two months in mild weather.

A Smart Birdbath

This interesting product pairs a plastic birdbath (on an optional metal stand) with a solar-powered camera, so you can keep an eye on visiting birds without having to deal with seed mess. When I first tested it, I was worried birds would splash water on the camera lens, but the most popular activity at the bath is by far drinking the water (birds, raccoons, squirrels … anything passing by). I don't love that the basin grows algae quickly and the pump clogs easily, but this is otherwise a very well-made item—it's been in my yard for a year and a half through every season, and while the plastic is starting to fade a bit, it's still going strong.

A Smart Nesting Box

Though I do love a smart bird feeder, Birdfy's Nest Duo is the absolute zenith of bird-watching for me. A black-capped chickadee moved in, laid eggs, and raised chicks (detailed here), and the cameras and app on the Nest stayed working, giving me 24-hour updates with interior night vision and views of the entry hole's exterior to see who was coming and going. A remote control on a 10-foot-long cord lets you reset or charge the camera without bothering the birds (though the auxiliary solar panel worked great for me). Note, however, that the black waterfall-style roof and lack of ventilation do pose a risk of overheating any young birds; during a May heat wave, I had to affix an umbrella and ice packs to the box, but the interior thermometer and hygrometer did a great job keeping me abreast of changing conditions.

entries.title: Which MacBook to Buy (2026): Here’s Which Laptop Is Right for You
entries.summary: With the introduction of the OLED MacBook Pro and MacBook Neo, there are now more Apple laptops than ever to choose from.
entries.content:
MacBooks went to some adventurous new places this year. The MacBook Neo pushes the boundaries of how cheap and low-powered a MacBook could go, while the OLED MacBook Pro takes it in the opposite direction. While the midyear price hike put a damper on all the new releases, prices won’t be going down anytime soon.

Having tested every new MacBook you can buy, I can guide you to the right laptop for your budget and performance needs.

For more recommendations, check out the rest of our computer buying guides, like Best Laptops, Best Mac Desktops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best iPads, and Best MacBook Accessories.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added notes from my testing of the M6 MacBook Pro and OLED MacBook Pros, along with additional buying advice given the new prices and rumors about future updates.

The MacBook for Most People

Although the MacBook Neo is more affordable, and the M5 MacBook Pro offers a better display with the far more powerful M5 Pro and Max chips, the MacBook Air remains the model I recommend for most people. The 2026 M5 refresh isn’t particularly exciting, but if your livelihood depends on sitting in front of a MacBook all day, it’s the best option.

The starting price for the 13-inch model is now $1,299, up $200 from before. Notably, for much of last year, you could buy this laptop for as little as $750. That’s a painful reality, but it doesn’t change my recommendation that this is the MacBook model most people should buy.

Although the exterior of the MacBook Air hasn’t changed since 2021, Apple has slowly evolved the laptop into something that feels airy and near-weightless. Most users need not worry about having too many tabs or applications open, eating up all that memory. You won’t be sitting around waiting for a file to download, because the SSD is blazing fast. With support for up to two 5K external monitors, the MacBook Air can function as a proper workstation when paired with a docking station. The 12-megapixel, 1080p webcam is plenty good for video calls.

What matters most is that the M5 can do far more than most people will ever ask of their MacBook Air. Apple has boosted the GPU so much over the past generations that the M5 is actually on par with the M3 Pro. You’ll probably spend most of your day in browser tabs, Slack, Zoom, office applications, and spreadsheets, but the MacBook Air can just as easily handle Photoshop or Lightroom. You can even dabble in video editing or some light gaming if you want. If you were a professional video editor, you’d likely be bothered by the render times. But if it’s more of a hobby or side project, the M5 MacBook Air likely won’t impede your flow. Again, that’s where the MacBook Air really lives up to its do-it-all reputation.

As always, there are two sizes, measured diagonally: 13.6-inch and 15.3-inch. Aside from the $200 price gap, the screen size and speakers are the only notable differences between the two. Apple even scales up the pixel density to make sure the display on the 15-inch model looks just as sharp. The speakers on the 15-inch model sound incredible, second only to the 16-inch MacBook Pro. But choosing between the two sizes really comes down to how you use your laptop. If you have it plugged into an external monitor most days, you may as well get the 13-inch model and save yourself the extra space when you need to carry it around. But if a laptop is your primary machine, having that 15.3-inch screen really makes a difference, especially for more complicated applications or for using Split View.

As you may notice, the M5 MacBook Air now starts with 512 GB of storage. That’s twice what previous models packed and helps to rationalize the price gap between the Neo and the Air. Having 512 GB of storage means you won’t have to worry about filling up your drive right away. This kind of headroom allows the technology to fade into the background—a design philosophy Apple has always championed. If you are a power user, consider adding more memory. Remember, MacBook memory and internal storage aren’t expandable down the road.

Read my in-depth comparison of the MacBook Neo and MacBook Air to see how they stack up.

The Best Pro MacBook

After years of rumors, Apple has launched a new MacBook Pro with never-before-seen features—most notably, the tandem PROLED XDR touchscreen. That’s right: this MacBook Pro is the first to ever have a touch-capable display, and you can now interact with it directly with your finger. Many people will be drawn in by the novelty of the feature (even though it’s been available on Windows laptops for almost a decade now), but I am skeptical about how useful it will be for day-to-day tasks. You will still primarily use the keyboard and trackpad, but I can see how the touchscreen would help in certain situations. Apple has made some optimizations to make the interface more touch-friendly, though I think there’s still room for improvement.

But don’t get me wrong: This MacBook Pro’s screen is the real deal. I’ve never seen a screen quite like this. Despite OLED’s reputation for not being bright enough, Apple’s is different. It delivers the insane contrast and clarity you’d expect from OLED, but with a maximum brightness that’s hundreds of nits higher than the previous-gen Mini-LED MacBook Pros.

It has a few tricks up its sleeve too, such as the return of the glow-up Apple logo on the lid and the hole-punch camera to replace the notch. As someone who has never gotten used to that ugly notch, that might be the change I was most thrilled to see. Apple even brought Dynamic Island from the iPhone to the MacBook Pro, using that hole creatively while hiding the camera. All in all, there’s a lot to be impressed by here.

The only real concern is that it still uses the older M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. These are still some of Apple’s most powerful chips, but they have been out for over a year. This is the first time Apple isn’t introducing new chips alongside its new MacBook Pro in the past six years. Rumors indicate that the company may be skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max altogether. That’s made stranger by the fact that Apple is keeping the previous-gen models in the lineup—another uncommon move.

There’s a $400 difference between the 2025 M5 Pro and the 2025 PROLED M5 Pro, and for this pro-level demographic of buyers, it’s a relatively small price to pay for all the upgrades. I appreciate that Apple kept the older models around for those who want the extra performance without the fancy, more expensive display. On the other hand, if Apple wasn’t currently selling them, third-party retailers might have dropped the price more while they were still in stock.

The Best MacBook for Students

The MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) came out earlier this year, and it had a lot to prove. That’s especially true since it debuted at just $599, an unheard-of price point for Apple laptops—much less than any other model, even before recent price hikes took effect. And even though the MacBook Neo now starts at $699 after those price increases, it remains an aggressively affordable option. To keep pricing low, Apple had to make the following compromises:

  • Only 8 GB of RAM;
  • A18 Pro mobile chip;
  • No backlit keyboard;
  • Outdated, slow USB-C ports;
  • Only supports one 4K external monitor;
  • No Touch ID (on $599 configuration);
  • Slower internal SSD;
  • Mechanical trackpad (instead of haptic).

That’s a big list, and the memory limitation is the most significant drawback. Unlike on the MacBook Air, you can find the limits of the Neo fairly easily—and not on purpose. If you’re coming from a 16 GB MacBook Air, for example, you likely developed a habit of keeping idle applications or tabs open. On the MacBook Neo, you’ll need to be a bit more aware of what’s open to avoid slowdowns. You’ll also want to know which ports you’re using, since only the rear USB-C port supports an external display. The other USB-C port is only USB 2.0, rated at a max of 480 megabits per second. That’s definitely not the one you want to use for file transfers. If you don’t have the Touch ID model, you may even need to watch who you’re sitting next to in a coffee shop when entering passwords. We haven’t had to worry about these things on laptops for many years.

In exchange, Apple delivers an incredible front-of-screen experience on the MacBook Neo, never before seen on a laptop of this price. The display is sharper and brighter than anything else you can buy for $699, while the keyboard and trackpad are both excellent. Build quality is every bit as strong as any other Apple product, and at 0.50 inches thick, it’s still quite portable.

On top of all that, the Neo has three really good features over the Air. There’s a wider range of color options—and a lot of people will gravitate toward the Neo for that alone. My favorite change is the lack of a camera notch. While the bezels are slightly thicker, I’d still prefer a uniform screen without an ugly notch blocking part of my view. Perhaps most meaningfully, the Neo is reportedly the most repairable MacBook in the lineup, swapping out adhesives for screws on components such as the battery and speakers. This is great for classrooms and businesses hoping to keep fleets of these up to date without contributing as much to the mounting e-waste problem.

For most of the time, you’ll enjoy using the MacBook Neo. As a parent, this should be the go-to device for high school and college students. It also works equally well as a secondary laptop away from your workstation or as a small travel laptop.

Previous-Gen MacBook Pros

The newer PROLED MacBook Pros are flashier, but they use the same M5 Pro or M5 Max chips as the previous-gen models. And interestingly, Apple still sells these older ones. So, while these 2025 models don’t have touchscreen OLED displays, they’re every bit as powerful. You aren’t missing out on any performance, and if the rumors hold, these will be the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro chips for a while.

Of course, these MacBook Pros are still very expensive, though. Like its PROLED sibling, the standard M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) aren’t for the average person. The price alone should clue you in, but if you are the target audience and willing to pay well over $4,000 for a powerful laptop, the M5 Max MacBook Pro is unmatched in its capabilities. As always, the “Max” is primarily about considerably more GPU performance. Along with the option of two extra CPU cores, you can get up to 40 GPU cores, each with a built-in AI accelerator.

The M5 Max’s power applies to three use cases: creative applications, on-device AI processing, and gaming. Whether it’s 3D modeling, video editing, or some other resource-heavy application, the M5 Max MacBook Pro will tear through it. But AI performance also takes a significant leap. I tested a 17-billion-parameter Llama-2 model, which ran at conversational speed locally (the speed an AI model runs on a device), and it was 31 percent faster than running the same model on the M3 Max MacBook Pro.

Then there’s gaming. Nobody is going to buy the MacBook Pro for its gaming prowess alone, but it’s there when you want it. For the first time ever, you can hit over 60 frames per second in Cyberpunk 2077 on the Ultra preset with no upscaling. That’s an RTX 5070 Ti-level of laptop gaming performance. And unlike laptops that actually have that GPU, the MacBook Pro gets incredible battery life. Lastly, creative professionals will appreciate the faster storage speeds than previous generations.

The Mini-LED display is as gorgeous as ever, even if it pales in comparison to the new OLED models. You get a solid selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 5 ports that offer ample external display support. It’s at the top of its class in nearly every aspect. Beyond CPU/GPU performance, you can choose between two screen sizes that perform similarly.

If this machine is overkill, you can drop down to the M5 Pro, which starts at $2,499 but is a power champ in its own right. Its multi-core and GPU performance are also stronger than the new M6 (see below).

The Awkward Middle Child

The MacBook Pro is a slight misnomer because there are really three variants. I’ve talked about the PROLED and M5 Pro/M5 Max versions above. The third, the base model, is the new M6 MacBook Pro, and despite using the latest chip, it’s the cheapest of the Pro options. Unfortunately, it’s also the hardest to recommend. That has less to do with the laptop itself and more to do with its price and how it fits into the lineup.

Like its M5 predecessor, it remains a beautiful, well-made laptop with all the high-end features you’d expect from a MacBook Pro. That includes the excellent speakers and very bright Mini-LED display. But it costs $1,999. Keep in mind that the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is $2,499, and you can still buy the M5 model for $1,799 or the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air for $1,499—hence the “awkward middle child” designation.

To be fair, you get a terabyte of storage and 16 GB of RAM, while the M5 MacBook Pro started with 512 GB of storage. Apple also kept the starting price the same—that is, the price after Apple increased pricing across the board (the base MacBook Pro used to start at $1,699), but let’s not go there.

The M6 chip is certainly faster than the M5, but it’s less of a big leap forward than in previous generations. You’re looking at about a 15 percent improvement in CPU performance. I think the bigger disappointment is only a 9 percent improvement in graphics. That’s been an area where previous generational chip leaps have been more significant.

If you are considering the M6 MacBook Pro, I strongly suggest you look at the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air. It starts at a much lower price for the base configuration, but you can bump up the specs and still stay below $2,000. Yes, the MacBook Air is a different machine, but it has the performance that would impress many MacBook Pro users.

A Breakdown of Each M-Series Chip

Apple’s processors are scattered across different MacBook models, and you can find older models online from third-party retailers, either new or refurbished. If you do stumble upon older chips, you might be wondering how they compare to newer options. Here, get a breakdown of the differences to consider.

M6 Series

M6: Apple has already released its latest M6 line of chips, though the rollout has been slower than normal. As of this year, it’s only available in the base 14-inch MacBook Pro, iMac, and Mac Mini. I expect to see this arrive on devices like the iPad Pro and MacBook Air eventually, but the rumors about the rest of the M6 lineup are perplexing. Reports indicate Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max entirely and jump straight to the M7 Pro and M7 Max, perhaps in late 2027. That makes sense given what Apple just launched with the OLED MacBook Pro, which uses the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the previous generation.

M5 Series

M5: Apple launched the M5 chips in late 2025 with the 14-inch MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and Vision Pro. The base M5 offers up to a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, though a lower-tier 9-core CPU is still available on the iPad Pro. The M5 is about 10 to 15 percent faster in CPU performance than the M4 and takes a significant step up in GPU, AI workloads, and even storage speed. The M5 is now also available on the MacBook Air.

M5 Pro: These more powerful M5 chips are currently available in the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros. The M5 Pro comes with a 15-core CPU and a 16-core GPU, with an option to upgrade to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. As with previous generations, the Pro chip gets all the same benefits as those in the M5 architecture but adds more cores and improved memory bandwidth. The biggest advantage is in GPU and on-device AI performance. This time around, however, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max also debuted the “Fusion Architecture,” a new version of UltraFusion (previously used only on the Ultra chips) that combines two dies across a superfast interconnect.

M5 Max: The M5 Max is the M5 Pro—only with more GPU power. You can get up to 40 GPU cores, putting the MacBook Pro on par with high-end gaming laptops in graphics performance. With neural accelerators built into each GPU core, you’ve got one of the most powerful AI laptops on the market. It comes in either the MacBook Pro or the Mac Studio.

M5 Ultra: Like the other “Ultra” chips, the M5 Ultra is available only in the 2026 Mac Studio. It’s by far Apple’s most powerful chip, but you can’t configure it in a MacBook.

M4 Series

M4: The M4 launched in 2024. It has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU. Apple claims the M4 delivers 1.8 times faster CPU performance and 2.2 times faster GPU performance than the M1. Meanwhile, the neural engine is more than three times faster than the original and twice as fast as the M3. It also starts with 16 GB of unified memory, which helps to power Apple Intelligence (the company’s suite of artificial intelligence features) more smoothly. It’s available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (2024), iMac (2024), and MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, 2025).

M4 Pro: The M4 Pro has a 14-core CPU (which Apple claims is up to 1.9 times faster than the M1 Pro) and up to a 20-core GPU, with up to 64 GB of unified memory. Built on a second-generation 3-nanometer process, it also supports enhanced GPU features like mesh shading and ray tracing—the latter of which is now twice as fast as on M3 chips. You’ll find it on the 2024 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) and Mac Mini (2024).

M4 Max: This chip has a 16-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU with support for up to 128 GB of unified memory. Apple says the CPU is up to 2.2 times faster than the M1 Max, while the GPU is up to 1.9 times faster. Like the M4 Pro, it supports mesh shading and ray tracing. The M4 Max is available as an option on the 2024 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro, and you can also get it as an option in the current Mac Studio.

M3 Series

M3: The M3 was available on the 14-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023), 13-inch MacBook Air (2024), 15-inch MacBook Air (2024), and 24-inch iMac (2023). It packs an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, with up to 24 GB of unified memory. Compared with the M1, Apple claimed CPU performance was up to 35 percent faster and GPU performance up to 65 percent faster. The company said the CPU and GPU are both 20 percent faster than the M2. As with the M1 and M2, it was great for basic tasks like word processing, sending emails, using spreadsheets, and light gaming. The 13-inch and 15-inch MacBook Air also supported two external displays (one up to 6K at 60 Hz and another up to 5K at 60 Hz).

M3 Pro: With a 12-core CPU and an 18-core GPU, Apple claimed the M3 Pro’s GPU was only up to 10 percent faster than the M2 Pro, making it a marginal upgrade from its predecessor. Compared with the M1 Pro, however, the M2 Pro was up to 40 percent faster in GPU performance and 20 percent faster in CPU performance. It was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2023. It was the ideal in-between for those who needed a chip more powerful than the M3 but didn’t need the full power of the M3 Max.

M3 Max: The next step up from the M2 Max. It had a 16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. According to Apple, the CPU performance was up to 80 percent faster than the M1 Max and up to 50 percent faster than the M2 Max. As for GPU performance, it was said to be up to 50 percent faster than the M1 Max and 20 percent faster than the M2 Max. The M3 Max was available on the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro (late 2023).

M3 Ultra: Apple introduced the M3 lineup in 2023, but only announced the M3 Ultra in 2025. It was even better than the latest M4 Max and M5 at the time. It had up to 32 CPU cores (24 performance cores) and up to 80 GPU cores. Apple claimed it was up to 2.5 times faster than the M1 Ultra. It also came with 96 GB of unified memory, upgradable to 512 GB, and up to 16 TB of SSD storage. This chip was available only on the 2025 Mac Studio.

M2 Series

M2: The M2 was an entry-level chip like the M1, with slightly more processing power. It packed an 8-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU (two more GPU cores than its predecessor), and supported up to 24 GB of unified memory. Apple said the second-generation chip has an 18 percent faster CPU and a GPU that’s 35 percent more powerful than its earlier version. The M2 was great for daily tasks like word processing and web browsing, but tasks such as editing multiple streams of 4K footage and 3D rendering should be reserved for Pro or Max chips. It was available in the MacBook Air (13-inch, 2022), MacBook Air (15-inch, 2022), and MacBook Pro (13-inch, 2022).

M2 Pro: The M2 Pro had up to 12 cores in the CPU and up to a 19-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple claimed performance was up to 20 percent faster than with the 10-core M1 Pro and graphics were 30 percent faster. We recommended this chip for intermediate video and photo editors. It was a marginal upgrade compared with the M1 Pro, but it was the best option for those who wanted a more future-proof processor. You could find it in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from early 2023 and the Mac Mini (2023).

M2 Max: The M2 Max packs up to a 12-core CPU and up to a 38-core GPU (with support for up to 96 GB of unified memory). According to Apple, graphics are 30 percent faster than on the M1 Max. The M2 Max is an excellent choice for those who work with graphics-intensive content, including graphic design, 3D modeling, and heavy-duty video footage. But as with the M2 Pro, it’s an incremental upgrade if you’re coming from an M1 Max. It’s available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) released in early 2023 and the Mac Studio (2023).

M2 Ultra: The successor to the M1 Ultra, the M2 Ultra was available in the second-generation Mac Studio and the Mac Pro (2023). Composed of two M2 Max chips, using Apple’s UltraFusion technology, the M2 Ultra had a 24-core CPU and a GPU configurable with 60 or 76 cores. Apple claimed the CPU delivered up to 20 percent faster performance and that the GPU was up to 30 percent faster than the M1 Ultra. This was the chip to get if you were working with extremely heavy-duty content that you believed the M1 Ultra, M2 Pro, or M2 Max simply couldn’t handle. You’d have known if you needed a chip this robust.

M1 Series

M1: Introduced in 2020, the M1 was Apple's first custom silicon designed for the Mac. The M1 had an 8-core CPU and up to an 8-core GPU. Originally, you could get up to 16 GB of unified memory (RAM) for an extra cost, but now you can only purchase the 8-GB model. It was much faster than any previous Intel-powered MacBook Pro and the practical choice for most people. It packed more than enough processing power for day-to-day tasks and even light gaming. It could also handle more intense jobs, like photo editing. Long after its initial release, Apple continued to sell the M1 MacBook Air through Walmart for just $599, a killer price for this laptop. The MacBook Neo has since replaced it, using the A18 Pro chip from the iPhone 16 Pro models.

M1 Pro: The next step up was the M1 Pro. It had up to 10 CPU cores and up to a 16-core GPU, with up to 32 GB of unified memory. Apple said the performance and graphics were both twice as fast as on the M1. We found it to be considerably more capable than the base chip, making it ideal for anyone who works heavily on MacBooks for music production or photo and video editing. Only the 2021 MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) used this chip.

M1 Max: Like the M1 Pro, the M1 Max had a 10-core CPU but a heftier 32-core GPU (with support for up to 64 GB of unified memory). Apple said it was four times faster than the M1 for graphics. As testing showed, this chip was extremely powerful and handled every heavy-duty task with ease. It was the go-to choice if you needed a computer that could handle multiple streams of 8K or 4K video footage, 3D rendering, or app development and demos. You probably already knew whether you needed this much power. It was available in the MacBook Pro (14-inch and 16-inch) from 2021.

M1 Ultra: The M1 Ultra was the most powerful of the M1 series. It’s two M1 Max chips connected with a technology called UltraFusion. It packs a 20-core CPU, 64-core GPU (configurable up to 128 GB of unified memory), and a 32-core neural engine—complete with seven times more transistors than the base M1. Even when newer models were available, the M1 Ultra remained powerful and a solid option for anyone who needs a heavy-duty processor for intense visuals and graphics work. It was available only on the first-generation Mac Studio.

Get AppleCare+ to Protect Your Devices

None of Apple’s MacBooks are cheap, and replacement parts are nightmarishly expensive. Advice on Buying Older MacBooks

You have to be very careful when shopping for older MacBooks. Don’t get me wrong: Since the introduction of Apple Silicon in 2020, almost every MacBook Air and MacBook Pro has been a really good laptop. Never buy a MacBook that predates 2020, regardless of how cheap it is. Trust me.

But even buying an older Apple Silicon model requires a discerning eye. Most older generations of MacBooks are sold only refurbished or secondhand, which adds risk. Meanwhile, prices on refurbished models fluctuate frequently, so you’ll need to watch prices closely to get the best deal. Apple’s own refurbished store prices are often higher than buying new models from third-party retailers like Amazon or Best Buy, but you do get some protection as they come with an Apple warranty. However, third-party retailers are always less risky than buying used on a secondhand market like Facebook Marketplace or eBay.

With that in mind, here are the older MacBooks you might see for sale, and whether I’d recommend buying.

MacBook Pro (M5): Apple doesn’t sell this one anymore, but some retailers are selling it at a discount for $1,799. That’s for 16 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. Since it’s nearly identical to the newer M6 MacBook Pro, except for a small performance bump, it’s a really good deal right now. I’d still say most people are better off getting a 15-inch MacBook Air because it’s cheaper and thinner, but if you want the better Mini-LED display, the M5 MacBook Pro is a solid choice right now.

MacBook Air (M4): The previous-generation MacBook Air is a fantastic laptop, but it’s no longer being sold new. However, you can now buy it refurbished for under $1,000. This configuration only comes with 256 GB of storage, though, and I don’t think it’s cheap enough to be worth it compared to the M5 model.

MacBook Air (M3): This one isn’t being sold new anymore, and the refurbished models I could find weren’t any cheaper than the M4 MacBook Air. Just stick with the M4.

MacBook Air (M2): With the launch of the MacBook Neo, there’s really no reason to buy an older MacBook Air with only 8 GB of RAM—especially at this price.

MacBook Air (M1): Thanks to the Neo, refurbished M1 MacBook Air models have sunk to pretty dramatic lows. You can currently buy a refurbished M1 for around $400. While the M1 MacBook Air gets you a backlit keyboard, the new MacBook Neo is certainly the more handsome and portable of the two. Still, if you need something fairly limited and are willing to risk buying refurbished, I can see why an Apple Silicon MacBook for less than $400 has its appeal.

MacBook Pro (14-inch, M4): This is no longer being sold new, but you can buy the refurbished model for $1,499. Earlier this year, you could have bought the M5 model for less than this. Sigh. Even still—definitely not worth it.

MacBook Pro (M3 Pro or M3 Max): Given how low the prices have dropped, these refurbished models may be worth considering, particularly for people who want a bit more performance than they’d get from a MacBook Air.

At this point, I do not recommend buying refurbished MacBook Pros from the M2 or M1 generation. I haven’t seen deals strong enough to justify buying something that old.
